gloss_terse: fearing, afraid (rare adjective describing one who fears or is in dread)
gloss_readable: This rare Hebrew adjective appears only twice, both times in Jeremiah describing those whom the prophet fears. The word captures the active state of being afraid or in dread of someone. Both occurrences use the same construction with the preposition 'from before them,' emphasizing the source of fear. The multilingual evidence shows consistent translation as 'fear' across languages, though some translators struggled with this rare form, leaving it untranslated.

senses.1: The adjective describes a person in a state of fear or dread. Both Jeremiah passages use identical phrasing: 'whom you fear from before them' (Jer 22:25, 39:17), referring to those the prophet dreads. The English 'fear' and Spanish 'temes' (you fear) capture the emotional state, while French and German translators left the Hebrew untranslated, perhaps uncertain of this rare adjectival form.

gloss_terse: to give thanks, to praise (Aramaic Haphel form used in Daniel for praising God)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic verb appears only in Daniel's prayers of thanksgiving to God. The Haphel stem (causative) suggests making acknowledgment or giving thanks publicly. Daniel uses this word when praising the God of heaven for revealing mysteries (Dan 2:23) and in his habit of daily prayer (Dan 6:10). The consistent multilingual rendering as 'giving thanks' or 'praising' reflects the liturgical context of both passages, showing Daniel's practice of gratitude even under threat of death.

senses.1: The verb describes formal acts of thanksgiving and praise directed to God. In Daniel 2:23, Daniel gives thanks to the God of his fathers for revealing Nebuchadnezzar's dream. In Daniel 6:10, the participle describes Daniel's ongoing practice of giving thanks before God three times daily. Spanish 'doy gracias' and French 'louer' (to praise) capture the devotional tone, while English emphasizes the participial aspect 'giving thanks, thanking.'

gloss_terse: Jedaiah (proper name: 'Yahweh has known'; Simeonite chief and Nehemiah-era builder)
gloss_readable: This personal name appears for two different individuals: a Simeonite clan chief listed in Chronicles and a builder who helped repair Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah. The name itself means 'Yahweh has known' or 'known by Yahweh,' reflecting the common Hebrew practice of embedding theological statements in names. The Septuagint's varied transliterations (Iedia, Ieddaa, Ieddeia) show the challenge of rendering Hebrew names in Greek, while modern translations generally settle on 'Jedaiah' in English.

senses.1: A proper name borne by at least two men in Israel's history. First, a chief in the tribe of Simeon (1 Chr 4:37), and second, one of the builders who repaired Jerusalem's wall alongside Nehemiah (Neh 3:10). The multilingual evidence shows standard transliteration practices: English 'Jedaiah' or 'Yedayah,' Spanish 'Jedaías' or 'Yedaya,' while French and German preserve the Hebrew form, reflecting uncertainty about vowel pointing in rare names.

gloss_terse: Yada (proper name: 'he knows/knew'; descendant of Judah in Chronicles genealogy)
gloss_readable: This brief personal name appears only in the genealogy of Judah's descendants, mentioned twice in rapid succession as a son of Onam (1 Chr 2:28, 32). The name derives from the common Hebrew root for 'to know,' and BDB notes that in Sabaean inscriptions it served as a royal epithet meaning 'the knowing one' or 'the shrewd one.' The name's simplicity and rarity have led most translators to simply transliterate it as 'Yada' across languages, preserving the Hebrew form.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in the Chronicler's genealogies of Judah, specifically as a descendant through Jerahmeel. The name occurs twice in the same genealogical context (1 Chr 2:28, 32), both times referring to the same individual. Most translations preserve the Hebrew form: English 'Yada,' Spanish 'Yada,' with French and German also maintaining the Hebrew spelling, since the name is too rare to have acquired a traditional rendering.

gloss_terse: YHWH-Nissi (proper name: 'The LORD is my banner'; altar name built by Moses after defeating Amalek)
gloss_readable: This compound name appears as the name Moses gave to an altar he built after Israel's victory over the Amalekites at Rephidim. The name combines the divine name with 'nissi' (my banner/standard), creating a theological declaration: 'The LORD is my banner.' In ancient warfare, a raised standard served as a rallying point for troops; Moses's altar name proclaims that Yahweh himself was Israel's rallying point and source of victory. The passage appears twice because of textual repetition in Exodus 17:15.

senses.1: The name Moses assigned to an altar commemorating God's role in Israel's defeat of Amalek (Exod 17:15, repeated twice in the same verse). The compound means 'Yahweh (is) my banner/standard,' with 'banner' (nes) referring to a military standard or rallying point. English preserves the elements: 'YHWH-Nissi' or 'The LORD is my banner,' Spanish 'Yahweh, estandarte mío,' and French 'l'Éternel, mon bannière,' all capturing the military metaphor of God as the rally point for his people.

gloss_terse: Jehoiarib (proper name: 'YHWH contends/pleads'; priestly family and individual names)
gloss_readable: This name appears in two variant spellings (Jehoiarib and Joiarib) for the same priestly family and other individuals. The name means 'Yahweh contends' or 'Yahweh pleads,' suggesting a family heritage tied to advocacy or legal defense. The name appears most prominently as the designation of one of the twenty-four priestly courses established under David, but also identifies a teacher in Ezra's time and a Judahite. The Septuagint's consistent transliteration across various forms (Ioiareib, Ioarib, etc.) reflects Greek attempts to capture the Hebrew.

senses.1: A proper name with variant spellings, most notably designating a priestly family course under David's organization (1 Chr 24:7). The occurrences in this batch show the name with conjunctions and prepositions: 'and Jehoiarib' and 'for Jehoiarib' (1 Chr 9:10, 24:7). Most translations transliterate consistently: English 'Jehoiarib' or 'Yehoyariv,' Spanish 'Yehoyarib,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew forms, acknowledging the name's multiple bearers across biblical history.

gloss_terse: Jehoaddah (proper name of uncertain meaning; descendant of Saul in Chronicles)
gloss_readable: This rare proper name appears only in the genealogies of Saul's descendants, mentioned twice in the same verse. The meaning remains disputed among scholars—possibilities include 'Yahweh has adorned,' 'Yahweh is equipment,' 'Yahweh has carried off spoil,' or even 'Yahweh has numbered.' The Septuagint's transliteration (Iada, Ioiada, Ioda) shows Greek translators were uncertain of the vowel pointing. A parallel passage in Chronicles gives the name as Jarah, suggesting possible textual corruption.

senses.1: A personal name appearing in the genealogy of Saul's descendants (1 Chr 8:36, twice in the same verse). The name's etymology is uncertain, though it clearly contains the divine element 'Yeho-' (Yahweh). Parallel passages give variant forms, suggesting textual uncertainty. English renderings vary: 'Jehoaddah' or 'Yehoadah,' Spanish 'Yehoada,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew consonantal form, reflecting the scholarly uncertainty about this rare name.

gloss_terse: Jehosheba (proper name: 'YHWH is an oath'; daughter of King Joram who saved infant Joash)
gloss_readable: This name appears in two spelling variants for the same remarkable woman: Jehosheba (2 Kings) and Jehoshabeath (2 Chronicles). She was King Joram's daughter and the wife of high priest Jehoiada, who courageously rescued her infant nephew Joash from Queen Athaliah's massacre of the royal family. The name means 'Yahweh is an oath' or 'Yahweh has sworn,' echoing the similar structure of Elizabeth (Elisheba). Her actions preserved the Davidic line at a critical moment in Judah's history.

senses.1: A proper name belonging to the daughter of Joram of Judah and wife of the priest Jehoiada. She appears twice in 2 Chronicles 22:11 with the longer spelling 'Jehoshabeath.' Her name means 'Yahweh is an oath,' parallel in structure to Elisheba. English uses 'Jehosheba' or 'Jehoshabeath,' Spanish 'Josaba,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew form. She is remembered for hiding the infant Joash from Athaliah's purge, thus preserving the messianic line.

gloss_terse: proud, arrogant, haughty (adjective describing presumptuous behavior)
gloss_readable: This Hebrew adjective appears only twice in wisdom and prophetic literature, both times characterizing arrogant persons who act with presumption. In Proverbs, it forms part of a triple description—'presumptuous, haughty, scoffer'—of someone who acts with overweening pride. In Habakkuk, it describes a man whose soul is not upright. The word captures the moral quality of arrogance that sets oneself above proper bounds, a vice consistently condemned in biblical wisdom literature.

senses.1: An adjective describing proud or arrogant character. In Proverbs 21:24, it appears in a triad: 'a presumptuous man, haughty, scoffer is his name,' describing one who acts with overflowing pride. In Habakkuk 2:5, it characterizes a man whose soul is not upright, contrasted with the righteous who live by faithfulness. The multilingual evidence is consistent: English 'arrogant,' Spanish 'arrogante,' French 'orgueilleux' (proud/haughty), all conveying moral disapprobation of self-exaltation.

gloss_terse: Jehallel'el (proper name: 'he shall praise God'; Judahite and Levite names)
gloss_readable: This theophoric name, meaning 'he shall praise God' or 'may he praise God,' appears for two different men: a descendant of Judah and a Levite who participated in Hezekiah's temple reforms. The name's form is parallel to the better-known Mahalalel, both built on the Hebrew root for 'praise.' The name embeds a declaration of worship, characteristic of many Hebrew personal names that serve as mini-theological statements about God's worthiness of praise.

senses.1: A proper name borne by two biblical figures: a man of Judah (1 Chr 4:16) and a Levite involved in cleansing the temple under Hezekiah (2 Chr 29:12). The name means 'he shall praise God' or 'may he praise God,' from the root 'halal' (to praise). Standard transliterations vary: English 'Jehallel'el' or 'Yehallelel,' Spanish 'Yehaleel' or 'Yehalelel,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew form, reflecting the name's rarity.

gloss_terse: Jocha (proper name; two different Benjamites in Chronicles)
gloss_readable: This rare personal name appears for two different Benjamite men in Chronicles genealogies and military lists. BDB notes that the form is equivalent to Juttah, possibly derived from the root 'to stretch' or 'extend.' The name's brevity and rarity have left translators uncertain about its vocalization, with variant readings in the textual tradition. The multilingual evidence shows diverse attempts to render this uncommon name, with some translations using 'Jocha' or 'Joha.'

senses.1: A proper name appearing in Benjamite genealogies and lists, identifying two different individuals: one in the family records (1 Chr 8:16) and another among David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:45). The name appears with the conjunction 'and Jocha' in both instances. Transliterations vary widely: English 'Jocha,' Spanish 'Yoja,' French and German preserve variant Hebrew forms ('Yocha,' 'Yicha'), reflecting textual uncertainty about this rare name's proper vocalization.

gloss_terse: Jochebed (proper name: 'YHWH is glory'; mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam)
gloss_readable: This significant name belongs to one of Scripture's most important mothers: the daughter of Levi who married Amram and bore Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. The name means 'Yahweh is glory' or 'glory of Yahweh,' making it one of the earliest biblical names to incorporate the divine name. Interestingly, this challenges some scholarly theories about when the divine name came into use. The name appears only twice, both in Priestly genealogies documenting the Levitical ancestry of Israel's great leaders.

senses.1: The proper name of Moses's mother, daughter of Levi and wife of Amram (Exod 6:20, Num 26:59, both from the Priestly source). The name means 'Yahweh is glory,' incorporating the divine name in a way that has sparked scholarly discussion about early Yahwism. Standard transliterations are remarkably consistent: English 'Jochebed,' Spanish 'Jocabed' or 'Yokeved,' French 'Jochebed' or 'Jokébed,' German 'Jochebed,' all preserving the name of this matriarch who gave birth to Israel's deliverer.

gloss_terse: mire, mud (noun describing deep mud or miry clay that entraps)
gloss_readable: This noun appears only in the Psalms, both times describing the treacherous mire or mud from which the psalmist cries for deliverance. The word captures the imagery of being stuck in deep, clinging mud that threatens to swallow one whole—a powerful metaphor for despair and mortal danger. Both occurrences use similar phrasing about being drawn up from or sinking into the miry clay. The etymology remains uncertain, though some scholars have proposed Persian or other origins.

senses.1: A noun denoting deep mud or mire that entraps. Both Psalm occurrences use vivid rescue imagery: drawn out 'from the miry clay' or 'pit of mud' (Ps 40:2) and sinking 'in deep mire' (Ps 69:2). The word appears with the article: 'the mud/mire.' Multilingual renderings show variety: English 'mire' or 'mud,' Spanish 'fango' (mud) or 'lodo' (mire), with translators capturing the sense of dangerous, entrapping muck from which only divine intervention can rescue.

gloss_terse: Joash (proper name: 'YHWH has aided'; Benjamite and royal officer names)
gloss_readable: This name, possibly meaning 'Yahweh has aided,' appears for multiple individuals throughout Scripture. In this batch we see two: a Benjamite son of Becher and an officer under David who supervised olive and sycamore groves. The name is shorter than the more common Jehoash but likely carries the same meaning, with the divine element providing hope that God assists or comes to help. The variety of men bearing this name reflects its popularity in ancient Israel.

senses.1: A proper name borne by several biblical figures, here appearing for a Benjamite son of Becher (1 Chr 7:8) and an officer in David's administration responsible for oil supplies (1 Chr 27:28). The name probably means 'Yahweh has aided,' from a root meaning 'to help.' Standard transliterations: English 'Joash' or 'Yoash,' Spanish 'Joás' or 'Yoás,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew form, distinguishing this name from the longer Jehoash.

gloss_terse: Jushab-hesed (proper name: 'kindness is returned'; son of Zerubbabel)
gloss_readable: This unusual compound name belongs to a son of Zerubbabel, the post-exilic governor who led the return from Babylon. The name appears twice in the same verse, apparently representing two separate elements that scribes treated as individual names: Jushab (meaning 'he returns' or 'he dwells') and Chesed (meaning 'kindness' or 'covenant loyalty'). The Septuagint's transliteration shows Greek translators struggled with this rare compound, producing very different renderings.

senses.1: A proper name (or possibly two separate names) appearing in Zerubbabel's genealogy (1 Chr 3:20, twice). The compound may mean 'kindness is returned' or 'dwelling in kindness.' Translators have handled it variously: some treat it as one name 'Jushab-hesed,' others as two separate names 'Jushab' and 'Chesed.' The multilingual evidence shows this division: English sometimes 'Jushav Chesed,' Spanish 'Yusab, Jesed,' reflecting the textual ambiguity of this rare Davidic descendant's name.

gloss_terse: Jehoshaphat (proper name: 'YHWH has judged'; king of Judah and other individuals)
gloss_readable: One of Scripture's most common personal names, meaning 'Yahweh has judged' or 'Yahweh judges.' The name appears most famously for the righteous king of Judah, son of Asa, but also for several other individuals including a priest, a military officer, and others. The name embeds a theological affirmation that God acts as judge, a theme central to Israel's faith. The two occurrences here show the name with conjunctions in Chronicles genealogies and service lists.

senses.1: A proper name with variant spellings (Jehoshaphat and Joshaphat) borne by multiple individuals. This batch shows two lesser-known bearers: one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:43) and a priest who blew trumpets before the ark (1 Chr 15:24), both appearing with the conjunction 'and Jehoshaphat.' The name means 'Yahweh has judged.' Standard transliterations: English 'Jehoshaphat' or 'Joshaphat,' Spanish 'Josafat' or 'Yosafat,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew, distinguishing these from the famous king of the same name.

gloss_terse: Jeziel/Jezuel (proper name, variant spellings; one of David's warriors at Ziklag)
gloss_readable: This name appears only once in the biblical text but in two variant textual forms (Ketiv and Qere), creating uncertainty about the proper spelling. The individual was one of the Benjamite warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in exile from Saul. The name's meaning is uncertain, though it may contain the divine element El. The textual variants (Jeziel vs. Jezuel) reflect ancient scribal uncertainty about the name's spelling, perhaps because this warrior was otherwise unknown.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in the list of warriors who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:3). The text preserves two variant readings: Ketiv (what is written) has one form, Qere (what is read) has another, both appearing in the same verse. The name may mean 'El sprinkles' or similar. Transliterations acknowledge the variants: English gives both 'Jeziel' and 'Jezuel' (in parentheses), with Spanish, French, and German similarly noting both forms, reflecting the textual uncertainty surrounding this obscure warrior's name.

gloss_terse: Jaazaniah (proper name: 'Yahweh hears'; multiple individuals, also contracted to Jezaniah)
gloss_readable: This name, meaning 'Yahweh hears,' appears in both full and contracted forms for several different individuals during the final days of Judah and the exile. The name expresses parental faith that God hears prayers—a common sentiment in Hebrew naming. The contracted form Jezaniah appears in Jeremiah's final chapters for individuals otherwise named Jaazaniah. The various individuals bearing this name include a Judean military leader, elders of Israel, and others during the traumatic period of Jerusalem's fall.

senses.1: A proper name borne by multiple individuals during Jeremiah's era, meaning 'Yahweh hears.' This batch shows contracted forms: 'and Jezaniah' and 'and Jezanyahu' (Jer 40:8, 42:1). The name appears in fuller form elsewhere as Jaazaniah. English transliterations vary: 'Jaazaniah,' 'Jezaniah,' 'Jezanyahu'; Spanish 'Jezanías' or 'Yezanyahu'; with French and German preserving the Hebrew contracted forms, reflecting the multiple individuals and spelling variants during Judah's final chaotic years.

gloss_terse: Chubbah (proper name; descendant of Asher, with Ketiv/Qere variant)
gloss_readable: This rare name appears only once in Asher's genealogy, and even there the text is uncertain. The Ketiv (written text) has one form while the Qere (reading tradition) suggests 'and Chubbah' with the conjunction. The name's meaning is uncertain—it may be related to a root meaning 'to hide' or 'to cherish.' The textual uncertainty and extreme rarity of this name have left translators divided on how to render it, with some preserving both readings.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in the genealogy of Asher (1 Chr 7:34, twice for Ketiv and Qere readings). The Qere suggests reading 'and Chubbah' (with conjunction) while the Ketiv lacks it. The name's etymology is uncertain. Transliterations show the textual division: English notes '[ketiv]' vs. 'and-Chubbah,' Spanish gives both readings in parentheses and brackets, with French and German preserving both Hebrew forms, acknowledging that we know almost nothing about this obscure Asherite beyond this genealogical mention.

gloss_terse: Jehdeyahu (proper name: 'may Yahweh give joy'; Levite and royal officer names)
gloss_readable: This name, meaning 'may Yahweh give joy' or 'Yahweh causes rejoicing,' reflects the hopeful prayers of parents at a child's birth. It appears for two individuals: a Levite in the temple service rosters and an officer under David who supervised the king's donkeys. The name's structure is characteristic of Hebrew names that embed petitions or declarations about what God does—in this case, bringing joy. The Septuagint's varied transliterations reflect Greek attempts to capture the Hebrew.

senses.1: A proper name appearing for two individuals: a Levite in David's organized temple service (1 Chr 24:20) and a royal officer in charge of David's donkeys (1 Chr 27:30). The name means 'may Yahweh give joy,' from the root for 'rejoicing.' Standard transliterations: English 'Jehdeyahu' or 'Yechdeyahu,' Spanish 'Jehedías' or 'Yejdeyahu,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew form, distinguishing these lesser-known officials from more prominent biblical figures.

gloss_terse: Jehieli (patronymic: 'of the Jehiel family'; Levitical family designation)
gloss_readable: This is not strictly a personal name but a patronymic—a family designation meaning 'of the family of Jehiel' or 'the Jehielite.' It appears in the Levitical genealogies describing the sons of Ladan who served in the temple treasury. Patronymics were important in ancient Israel for establishing family connections and inheritance rights, especially for Levitical families whose service assignments were organized by ancestral houses. The term identifies descendants or clan members of someone named Jehiel.

senses.1: A patronymic (family designation) appearing in Levitical records (1 Chr 26:21, 22), meaning 'of the Jehieli (family)' or 'the Jehielites.' The term identifies members of a Levitical family descended from Jehiel who served in the temple treasuries. Transliterations are relatively consistent: English 'Jehieli,' Spanish 'Jehieli,' with French and German preserving the Hebrew form. The Septuagint omits it in one verse, suggesting Greek translators found the patronymic designation difficult to represent.

gloss_terse: Jahleel (proper name: 'wait for God!' or 'God waits'; son of Zebulun)
gloss_readable: This name, meaning 'wait for God' or possibly 'may God wait,' belongs to one of the sons of Zebulun listed in Genesis and Numbers. The name embeds a theological exhortation or petition related to hope and patience in God. Names built on the root 'to wait' or 'to hope' reflect the virtue of patient trust that characterized biblical faith. The name appears in both patriarchal genealogies and tribal census lists, establishing Jahleel as a clan founder within Zebulun.

senses.1: A proper name belonging to a son of Zebulun and founder of a clan (Gen 46:14, Num 26:26). The name means 'wait for God!' or 'hope in God,' built on the root for waiting/hoping. The two occurrences show the name with prepositions: 'and Jahleel' and 'to Jahleel' (referring to his clan). Standard transliterations: English 'Jahleel,' Spanish 'Yahleel' or 'Yajleel,' French and German 'Jahleel,' with multilingual evidence showing consistent understanding of this Zebulunite clan founder.

gloss_terse: roebuck (animal: a deer species, possibly gazelle, permitted as clean food)
gloss_readable: This noun designates a species of deer or gazelle permitted as clean food under Mosaic law. The word appears in lists of edible animals in Deuteronomy and provisions for Solomon's table. Ancient cognates in Samaritan, Syriac, and Targumic Aramaic confirm the identification with a reddish-colored deer. Modern scholars have identified it with the roebuck based on descriptions from 19th-century naturalists who observed the species in Palestine. The name apparently derives from its reddish coloring.

senses.1: A noun denoting the roebuck, a species of deer permitted as food (Deut 14:5, 1 Kgs 4:23). Deuteronomy lists it among clean animals, while Kings includes it in the daily provisions for Solomon's royal table. Both occurrences use 'and roebuck(s)' with the conjunction. Multilingual renderings: English 'roebuck(s),' Spanish 'gamo' (fallow deer), French and German preserve the transliteration, though 19th-century naturalists confirmed this as the roebuck species, noted for reddish coloring and presence in biblical-era Palestine.

gloss_terse: Jahzeel (proper name: 'God apportions/divides'; son of Naphtali)
gloss_readable: This name, meaning 'God divides' or 'God apportions,' belongs to a son of Naphtali and founder of a clan. The name appears in variant spellings (Jahzeel and Jahziel) across different biblical passages, reflecting the challenges of preserving rare names through scribal transmission. The theological content is significant: the name affirms God's role in distribution and apportionment, perhaps reflecting gratitude for the land inheritance or family portion. The Septuagint's varied transliterations show Greek translators were uncertain about the vowel pointing.

senses.1: A proper name belonging to a son of Naphtali and clan founder, appearing with variant spellings across texts (Gen 46:24, Num 26:48, = Jahziel in 1 Chr 7:13). The name means 'God divides' or 'God apportions.' This batch shows prepositional forms: 'to Jahzeel' and 'Jahzeel.' Standard transliterations vary: English 'Jahzeel,' Spanish 'Yajtsel' or 'Yahseel,' French and German 'Jahzeel,' all acknowledging this Naphtalite clan founder whose name affirms divine providence in apportionment.

gloss_terse: Juttah (proper name: town in Judah's hill country, assigned to priests)
gloss_readable: This place name designates a town in the hill country of Judah that was later assigned to the priests as a Levitical city. The name appears in two variant spellings in the Masoretic tradition, though both likely refer to the same location. The town's precise location is uncertain, though it was in the Judean highlands. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to stretch out' or 'extend,' possibly describing the town's geographic situation or founding.

senses.1: A proper name designating a town in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:55) that was later assigned to the priests as a Levitical city (Josh 21:16). The two occurrences show prepositional forms: 'Juttah' and 'and Juttah.' The name appears with slight spelling variants in the Hebrew tradition. Standard transliterations: English 'Juttah' or 'Yuttah,' Spanish 'Jutá,' French and German 'Juttah' or 'Yuttah,' identifying this priestly city in Judah's highlands.

gloss_terse: scab, scurf (skin disease: eruptive condition that disqualified priests from service)
gloss_readable: This medical term appears only in Levitical purity laws, designating some kind of eruptive skin disease. Both occurrences appear alongside another skin condition (garab), suggesting these were related or commonly paired ailments. The disease was serious enough to disqualify priests from offering sacrifices and to render animals unfit as offerings. The precise medical identification is uncertain—it may have been some kind of scaly eruption, scab, or scurf. Ancient translators apparently understood it as a skin affliction but weren't more specific.

senses.1: A noun denoting a skin disease, possibly scab or scurf, that rendered priests unfit for service (Lev 21:20) and animals unsuitable for sacrifice (Lev 22:22). Both occurrences pair it with another skin condition (garab), suggesting related conditions. Multilingual renderings show uncertainty: English 'a skin disease,' Spanish 'empeines' (skin eruptions/eczema), French 'une maladie de peau' (a skin disease), German 'ein Haut-Krankheit' (a skin disease)—all indicating eruptive skin conditions without precise medical identification.

gloss_terse: the sea (Aramaic noun used in Daniel's vision of beasts from the great sea)
gloss_readable: This is the Aramaic word for 'sea,' appearing only in Daniel's apocalyptic vision of four beasts rising from the great sea. The word is cognate to the Hebrew 'yam' and appears in Syriac and Targumic Aramaic with the same meaning. In Daniel 7, the sea represents chaos and the realm from which hostile kingdoms emerge in God's prophetic timetable. Both occurrences appear with the Aramaic emphatic state (definite article), referring to 'the sea' as a specific cosmic symbol.

senses.1: An Aramaic noun meaning 'sea,' appearing in Daniel's vision of the four beasts (Dan 7:2, 3). The vision describes the four winds churning up 'the great sea' from which four beasts emerge, representing successive empires. Both occurrences use the emphatic/definite form 'yamma' (the sea). Multilingual renderings are consistent: English 'the sea,' Spanish 'el mar' or 'hacia el mar' (toward the sea), confirming understanding of this Aramaic term for the chaotic sea from which Daniel's beasts arise.

gloss_terse: Jemuel (proper name; son of Simeon, called Nemuel in other passages)
gloss_readable: This name belongs to a son of Simeon and appears in the Genesis and Exodus genealogies. Interestingly, in parallel passages in Numbers and Chronicles, the same individual is called Nemuel, suggesting either textual variants or a deliberate name change. The name's meaning is uncertain, though it contains the element 'El' (God). The variation between Jemuel and Nemuel reflects the kinds of scribal variations that occurred in preserving genealogical records over centuries of transmission.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in Simeon's genealogy (Gen 46:10, Exod 6:15), identified in BDB as the same person called Nemuel in Numbers 26:12 and 1 Chronicles 4:24. The name may mean 'day of God' or similar, though etymology is uncertain. Standard transliterations: English 'Jemuel,' Spanish 'Yemuel,' French and German 'Jemuel,' all identifying this Simeonite clan founder whose name varies in parallel biblical genealogies.

gloss_terse: the right (adjective: Ketiv form meaning 'right-hand' or 'on the right side')
gloss_readable: This is a Ketiv (written) textual variant of the adjective for 'right' or 'right-hand,' appearing where the Qere (reading tradition) suggests a different vocalization. Both occurrences involve positioning or directionality: the pillar on the right side of the temple (2 Chr 3:17) and Ezekiel lying on his right side (Ezek 4:6). The variant reflects scribal traditions about how to vocalize the adjective. The difference is minor—both forms communicate 'right' or 'right-hand.'

senses.1: An adjectival form (Ketiv reading) meaning 'the right (one)' or 'the right (side),' appearing in passages where the Qere suggests reading 'hayemani' instead. The occurrences describe the right pillar of Solomon's temple (2 Chr 3:17) and Ezekiel's right side (Ezek 4:6). Multilingual evidence shows understanding of 'right' direction: English notes the Ketiv variant, Spanish similarly brackets the Ketiv form, French and German preserve the Hebrew, all acknowledging textual variants in representing this common directional adjective.

gloss_terse: Jaminite (gentilic: 'belonging to the clan of Jamin'; also used for Benjamite)
gloss_readable: This gentilic (ethnic/clan designation) has two uses: as a patronymic for the clan of Jamin, son of Simeon, and apparently also as a designation for Benjamites. The word's dual usage is unusual—it may reflect different Hebrew traditions or homonyms. In Numbers it clearly designates Jamin's clan, while in 2 Samuel it apparently describes a Benjamite, creating some scholarly puzzlement. Gentilics were important for establishing tribal and clan identity in ancient Israel.

senses.1: A gentilic (clan designation) with two apparently distinct uses: 'the Jaminites' (clan of Jamin, son of Simeon, Num 26:12) and possibly 'Benjamite' (2 Sam 20:1, though this is debated). The term appears with the article as a collective. Transliterations show the ambiguity: English 'the Jaminite' or 'Yemini,' Spanish 'benjamita' (Benjamite) or 'los yaminitas,' with French and German similarly varying, reflecting scholarly uncertainty whether this represents one term with two meanings or two homonyms.

gloss_terse: Janoah (proper name: town on Ephraim's border, possibly meaning 'resting place')
gloss_readable: This place name designates a town on the border of Ephraim mentioned in Joshua's territorial descriptions. The name appears twice in quick succession, describing the border's course from one point to Janoah. Modern scholars have identified it with Yanun, southeast of Shechem, based on the geographic descriptions and archaeological evidence. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to rest' or 'to settle,' suggesting it was a resting place or settled location along the border.

senses.1: A proper place name appearing in Ephraim's border description (Josh 16:6, 7), identified with modern Yanun southeast of Shechem. Both occurrences use prepositional forms: 'Janoah' and 'from Janoah,' describing the territorial boundary. Standard transliterations: English 'Janoah' or 'Yanoach,' Spanish 'Janoa,' French and German 'Yanoach,' all identifying this Ephraimite border town whose name may mean 'resting place,' fitting its geographic role as a boundary marker.

gloss_terse: Janum (proper name: town in Judah's hill country, with Ketiv/Qere textual variants)
gloss_readable: This place name appears in Joshua's list of towns in Judah's hill country, but the text itself is uncertain. The Ketiv (written text) and Qere (reading tradition) preserve different forms, suggesting ancient uncertainty about the name's spelling or pronunciation. The town's location is unknown, and it appears only in this one list. The textual variants have left translators uncertain whether to read 'Janum' or 'Janim,' with modern translations acknowledging both possibilities.

senses.1: A proper place name in Judah's hill country (Josh 15:53, appearing twice for Ketiv and Qere variants). The written text (Ketiv) has one form while the reading tradition (Qere) suggests another, creating uncertainty about the town's name. Most likely 'Janum' though 'Janim' is also possible. Transliterations acknowledge the variants: English notes '[ketiv]' and 'Janum,' Spanish gives both in parentheses and brackets, with French and German similarly preserving both forms, reflecting ancient uncertainty about this otherwise unknown Judean town.

gloss_terse: Iddo (proper name: prophet/seer in Chronicles, with Ketiv/Qere textual variants)
gloss_readable: This proper name appears with textual variants (Ketiv vs. Qere) for a prophet or seer whose writings are mentioned as a source for Solomon's acts. The name Iddo appears elsewhere in Chronicles for various individuals—a seer whose visions concerned Jeroboam, among others. The textual uncertainty (Yedo vs. Yedai in the variants) reflects scribal traditions about how to vocalize this name. The individual was significant enough that his prophetic writings were used as historical sources by the Chronicler.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in reference to prophetic writings about Solomon (2 Chr 9:29, twice for Ketiv and Qere variants). BDB identifies this with Iddo the seer mentioned elsewhere in Chronicles. The Qere suggests reading 'Yedo' while the Ketiv has a slightly different form. Transliterations reflect the variants: English 'Iddo' or notes the variants 'Yedo/Yedai,' Spanish and French/German similarly preserve both Hebrew forms, acknowledging ancient uncertainty about the exact vocalization of this prophetic source's name.

gloss_terse: Jair (proper name: father of Elhanan, with Ketiv/Qere variants)
gloss_readable: This name appears with textual uncertainty (Ketiv vs. Qere) for the father of Elhanan, one of David's warriors who killed a giant. The parallel passage in 2 Samuel has been corrupted, and scholars suggest reading 'Jair' (as Chronicles has it) for the garbled 'Jaare-oregim' in Samuel. The name itself is well-attested elsewhere in Scripture, meaning possibly 'he enlightens' or 'Yahweh enlightens.' The textual variants here are minor—both forms point to the same name with slight spelling differences.

senses.1: A proper name appearing for the father of Elhanan the giant-slayer (1 Chr 20:5, twice for Ketiv and Qere variants). BDB notes the parallel 2 Samuel 21:19 passage is corrupt. The Qere reading 'Yair' is preferred over the Ketiv 'Yaor.' Transliterations acknowledge the variants: English 'Jair' with note of Ketiv, Spanish gives both forms in parentheses, French and German preserve both Hebrew variants, identifying this warrior's father despite ancient scribal uncertainty about spelling.

gloss_terse: Jaaziyahu (proper name: Levite name, possibly corruption of Uzziyahu)
gloss_readable: This Levitical name appears only in the priestly course listings in Chronicles, and scholars suspect it may be a textual corruption of the more common name Uzziyahu (Uzziah). The name as it stands would mean something like 'Yahweh makes bold' or 'Yahweh strengthens,' but the suggestion of textual corruption is based on the name's rarity and similarity to other names. Both occurrences appear with prepositions in the Levitical genealogies describing family leadership.

senses.1: A proper Levitical name appearing in priestly genealogies (1 Chr 24:26, 27), possibly a textual corruption of Uzziyahu according to some scholars. The occurrences show prepositional forms: 'Jaaziyahu' and 'for/to Jaaziyahu.' If genuine, the name would mean 'Yahweh emboldens' or similar. Transliterations preserve the Hebrew: English 'Jaaziyahu' or 'Yaaziyahu,' Spanish 'Yaaziyahu,' French and German maintain the Hebrew form, acknowledging this rare (possibly corrupt) Levitical name whose exact form remains uncertain.

gloss_terse: counselors (Aramaic plural noun: royal advisors to the Persian king)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic term appears only in Ezra, designating the counselors or advisors to the Persian king. The word is a plural noun with pronominal suffix ('his counselors'), referring to the advisors who, along with the king, sent Ezra back to Jerusalem with authority and resources. The term reflects the administrative structure of the Persian Empire, where the king ruled with a council of advisors. Both occurrences describe Ezra's authorization coming from the king and his counselors together.

senses.1: An Aramaic plural noun meaning 'counselors' or 'advisors,' appearing with the pronominal suffix 'his counselors' (Ezra 7:14, 15), referring to the Persian king's advisory council. The term describes those who, with the king, authorized Ezra's mission to Jerusalem. Multilingual renderings are consistent: English 'counselors' or 'his counselors,' Spanish 'consejeros' (counselors) or 'sus consejeros' (his counselors), reflecting understanding of this Aramaic term for the royal advisory body in the Persian imperial administration.

gloss_terse: Jeush (proper name: 'he comes to help'; son of Esau and other individuals)
gloss_readable: This name, possibly meaning 'he comes to help' or related to an Arabian divine name, appears for multiple individuals, most notably a son of Esau by Oholibamah. The name occurs with variant spellings (Ketiv vs. Qere) in several passages, reflecting ancient uncertainty about vowel pointing. It's borne by an Edomite chief, Benjamites, a Levite, and a son of Rehoboam. The name's etymology is disputed—it may reflect Arabian influence or be a purely Hebrew formation about divine help.

senses.1: A proper name appearing for multiple individuals, here shown for Esau's son (Gen 36:5, 14). Both occurrences show Ketiv spelling variants. The name possibly means 'he comes to help' or may derive from Arabian divine names. Standard transliterations vary: English often 'Jeush,' Spanish notes textual variants, German 'Jeusch,' acknowledging the Ketiv/Qere differences. The name identifies an Edomite chief among other biblical figures, its exact etymology remaining scholarly debate between Hebrew and Arabian origins.

gloss_terse: Jaala (proper name: head of returning exiles, with variant spelling Jaalah)
gloss_readable: This name appears in the lists of temple servants who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. The name occurs in two variant spellings—Jaala in one list and Jaalah in the parallel list, reflecting the common phenomenon where Ezra and Nehemiah preserve slightly different forms of the same names. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to climb' or 'to be high,' possibly a reference to mountain goats. Both forms refer to the same family head.

senses.1: A proper name appearing for the head of a family of temple servants who returned from exile, with variant spellings: 'Jaalah' in Ezra 2:56 and 'Jaala' in Nehemiah 7:58. The spelling variation is typical of parallel Ezra-Nehemiah lists. Transliterations show the variance: English 'Jaala' or 'Jaalah,' Spanish 'Jaalá' (combining both), French and German preserve both Hebrew forms, acknowledging these represent the same family leader whose name was spelled differently in the two return lists.

gloss_terse: ostriches (plural noun: large flightless birds, with Ketiv/Qere textual variant)
gloss_readable: This rare plural noun appears only in Lamentations, where the text compares the cruelty of Jerusalem's people to ostriches in the wilderness. The word appears with a Ketiv/Qere variant—the written text has one form while the reading tradition suggests 'like ostriches.' The ostrich was proverbial in biblical literature for abandoning its young, making it a fitting image for the breakdown of natural affection during Jerusalem's siege. The word may derive from a root suggesting voraciousness.

senses.1: A plural noun meaning 'ostriches,' appearing in Lamentations 4:3 with Ketiv/Qere variants. The Ketiv (written) has one form while the Qere (read) suggests 'like ostriches' (with comparative particle). The context compares the harshness of Jerusalem's people to ostriches, birds known for apparent cruelty to their young. Multilingual renderings show the comparison: English '(like) ostriches' with brackets noting variants, Spanish 'como avestruces' (like ostriches), French and German preserve both textual forms, conveying this poignant image of unnatural cruelty.

gloss_terse: Jarah (proper name: descendant of Saul, possibly corrupt text for Jehoaddah)
gloss_readable: This name appears only in the genealogy of Saul's descendants in Chronicles, but scholars widely regard it as a textual corruption of Jehoaddah, which appears in the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 8. The name as it stands would derive from a root meaning 'forest' or 'honeycomb,' but the scholarly consensus favors seeing it as a scribal error. Both occurrences appear in the same verse in the genealogical record, representing the repeated name structure common in biblical genealogies.

senses.1: A proper name appearing in Saul's genealogy (1 Chr 9:42, twice), which BDB identifies as probably corrupt for 'Jehoaddah' based on the parallel in 1 Chronicles 8:36. If genuine, it would mean 'forest' or similar. Transliterations preserve the form: English 'Jarah' or 'Yarah,' Spanish 'Yaara,' French and German maintain the Hebrew, though most scholars consider this a scribal error for the name that appears in the parallel genealogy. The textual uncertainty leaves the true name of this Saulide descendant in doubt.
